# Quiet Sonar Playbook

## Hiding

When choosing where to hide, avoid the extreme edges (1 and 9) as they're easier to target systematically. Position yourself in the middle ranges (4-6) where you have room to maneuver.

When you've survived a round in a particular cell without being hit, don't assume that cell is safe for the next round—move away from it unless you have strong evidence it will be avoided by all players.

When analyzing opponent firing patterns across multiple rounds, look for cells they've fired at repeatedly without claiming hits. These are likely cells they've already checked and don't expect targets to hide in. Avoid hiding there since it suggests they may circle back or it's otherwise disadvantageous.

## Firing

When choosing where to fire in early rounds, select a mid-range cell (around 5-7) to establish an aggressive presence without overcommitting to any particular hypothesis about opponent positions.

Don't repeat the same fire cell across consecutive rounds unless you have evidence suggesting that cell is productive. Vary your shots to gather information.

In final rounds when you're ahead in points, don't take unnecessary risks by firing at cells you haven't successfully hit before. A conservative fire choice that doesn't damage your credibility is better than a desperate high-value gamble.

## Claiming

Always claim the truth about whether you hit or missed. Never lie about the outcome.

The cost of false claims exceeds any benefit: it damages your credibility, and in a game where all fires are public, you risk being exposed if your claim contradicts observable evidence. Truth-claiming builds trust that makes other players more predictable and keeps you focused on strategy rather than keeping track of lies.

# Quiet Sonar Playbook

## Hide Strategy

When choosing where to hide my submarine, I should avoid clustering with other players' revealed firing patterns. If my opponent has claimed hits at certain positions or repeatedly fires at a narrow range, I hide outside that range rather than within it—they may be testing expanded positions or adapting after failed shots there.

In early rounds with no information, I pick a middle position (4-6 range) as a reasonable default that doesn't signal extremes.

## Fire Strategy

When firing at my target, I should pick positions based on observed hiding patterns from previous rounds, not intuition about "strong" or "weak" shots. Without evidence of where my target hides, firing at the middle range (5-7) is as good as anywhere else.

I should track whether my target tends to hide at certain positions across rounds and adjust my fire toward those positions in later rounds.

## Claim Strategy

I always claim the truth about whether I hit or missed. False claims risk credibility damage if detected, provide minimal strategic benefit (the fire is already public and my target knows the truth), and don't compound my scoring advantage when I do hit. Honesty is the dominant strategy in a multi-round game where reputation affects how other players perceive my reliability.

## What Did Not Work

Picking a fire position (7 in the final round) without analyzing my target's actual hide locations from previous rounds achieved nothing. I should have reviewed where Gamma actually hid before firing, not guessed at a "strong" number.

# Quiet Sonar Playbook

**HIDING STRATEGY**

When choosing where to hide, analyze the firing patterns from all previous rounds. Track which cells have been targeted most frequently across the board. Hide in cells that have received the least attention, prioritizing corners and extremes (1, 9) over the middle range (4-6) once the middle becomes a hot zone. Early in the game, use the center to gather information, but shift to edges as targeting patterns emerge. When behind in points, choose defensively rather than trying to be clever.

**FIRING STRATEGY**

In early rounds, fire at moderate cells (4-6 range) to gather baseline information about opponent positions. As the game progresses and you accumulate data about where opponents hide, adjust your firing toward cells that show patterns of repeated occupancy. In the final round, you can afford to be aggressive since no future retaliation follows. Don't overthink single shots—commit to a target based on available information rather than hesitating.

**CLAIMING STRATEGY**

Always claim the true result. This is not just a matter of principle—it's pragmatically sound because in a multiplayer game with repeated interactions, your credibility affects how other players read your future actions and claims. Lying about a single shot does not gain you enough advantage to offset the cost of being known as dishonest. Even in the final round when there's no reputation consequence ahead, maintain truthful claiming to avoid building bad habits.

**ADAPTATION**

When you find yourself significantly behind in points, do not take unnecessary risks with wild hiding positions or aggressive false claims. Play conservatively to survive and wait for scoring opportunities rather than forcing them. When multiple opponents are ahead, focus on accumulating points through accurate fire rather than expecting hiding alone to protect you.

# Quiet Sonar Playbook

## Hiding Strategy

When choosing where to hide my submarine, I will avoid the center cell and the corners initially, as these are predictable anchor points. I will instead select from the middle ranges (3-7), varying my position across rounds to remain unpredictable.

When I notice that my target has fired at specific cells multiple times with claimed hits, I will avoid those cells since they indicate where my target believes I've been hiding.

When analyzing the firing patterns of other players over multiple rounds, I will identify clusters of shots (cells 5-7 in my episode) and assume that successful hits were concentrated in those ranges, then move away from them.

## Firing Strategy

When firing at my target in early rounds, I will use middle-range cells (5-7) as a balanced approach rather than committing to specific patterns too early.

When I miss a shot, I will not immediately fire at nearby cells in the next round; instead, I will vary my firing range to explore different areas of the board.

When I notice I'm behind on points significantly, I will not change my strategy to become more aggressive or reckless—maintaining consistent methodology is more important than chasing points.

## Claiming Strategy

When the referee tells me I've missed my shot, I will always claim miss, regardless of strategic pressure or being behind on points. Claiming falsely creates a public record that can be contradicted and damages my credibility with other players for the entire remaining game.

When all fires are public, I will recognize that false claims have nowhere to hide and will always match my claim to my true result.

When I'm in the final rounds, I will maintain truthful claims even more strictly, since endgame interactions depend on established trust.

## Scoring Mindset

I will accept that a score of +3 in a multiplayer game where I'm competing against three other players is a reasonable outcome, not a failure. I will not let being in last place pressure me into deceptive plays.

I will recognize that maintaining integrity across all six rounds is worth more than a single gain from one false claim.
